Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the first page of an onboarding document for a new backend engineer joining a payments team. Around 200 words.

# Welcome to payments

You're joining a team that processes transactions for millions of users. The systems here move money reliably, which means we optimize for correctness first, speed second.

Read the architecture doc in the wiki. It outlines our service boundaries: the ledger service (source of truth for account balances), the gateway (external payment processor integration), and the reconciliation job (catches any divergence between the two). Most backend work touches one of these three.

Your first task is to set up local development. The README in the payments repo has setup steps. Do them, then run the full test suite. It should pass in under 2 minutes. If it doesn't, that's a signal we have a problem—file an issue with the exact error and tag @backend-oncall.

Spend tomorrow reading the last 10 merged pull requests. You'll see our code style, naming conventions, and the kinds of decisions we debate. Open a PR with questions in the comments. We want you asking.

The payments integration tests run against a sandbox account with our processor, not mocks. You have access. Use it to verify your changes. If you break something, it only affects the sandbox.

You'll pair with whoever merged your first PR. Grab 2 hours on their calendar this week. Payments has sharp edges. Learning them directly beats discovering them in production.

The text above has these problems. Rewrite it so none remain.
Change nothing else, and keep the same length and purpose.

- colon_reveal (It outlines our service boundaries:):
- paragraph_uniformity (6 paragraphs, spread 0.28):

Return only the rewritten text.

Read the architecture doc in the wiki. Our three core services are the ledger (source of truth for account balances), the gateway (external payment processor integration), and the reconciliation job (catches any divergence between the two). Most backend work touches one of these.

Your first task is local development setup. The README in the payments repo has the steps. Run the full test suite when done—it should pass in under 2 minutes. If it doesn't, file an issue with the exact error and tag @backend-oncall. That signals a problem we need to fix.

Tomorrow, read the last 10 merged pull requests to absorb our code style, naming conventions, and how we debate decisions. Open a PR with questions in the comments. We want you asking.

The payments integration tests run against a sandbox account with our processor, not mocks. You can verify your changes without risk to production.

This week, grab 2 hours on the calendar of whoever merges your first PR. You'll pair to learn the sharp edges directly—getting them wrong in production is expensive.
